evidence: backend/servers/reality-server/src/routes/price_map.rs:32-38 — PRICE_MAP_CACHE is a process-global `HashMap<String, CacheEntry>` (OnceLock<Arc<RwLock<..>>>) with NO size cap and NO eviction policy other than TTL expiry. The map key embeds raw, attacker-controlled request parameters: cache_key = format!("{}:{}:{}:{}", mode, time_window_str, query.property_type.unwrap_or(""), query.city.unwrap_or("")) at :125-131, where `query.city` and `query.property_type` are free-form strings taken straight off the public, UNAUTHENTICATED GET /api/v1/price-map handler (`get_price_map(State, Query<PriceMapQuery>)` at :97-100 — no RequestPrincipal / no auth extractor).

Memory-exhaustion DoS: the only reclamation is `cache.retain(|_, v| Instant::now() < v.expires_at)` at :229 run on the write path, and CACHE_TTL = Duration::from_secs(3600) (:41). Because entries live a full hour before they become eligible for retain to drop them, an attacker issuing GET /api/v1/price-map?city=<unique-random-string> on a loop inserts a brand-new, never-expiring-within-the-window entry on every distinct city value (:227-234 unconditionally `cache.insert(cache_key, CacheEntry{..})`). Each `city` only has to differ by one byte; it does not need to match any real listing (the query runs `city ILIKE $3` and caches even an empty district vector). Millions of distinct keys accumulate within the 1h TTL → unbounded heap growth → OOM on a public endpoint.

This is a self-inconsistency the codebase already knows how to avoid: the sibling anonymous-abuse surface in state.rs:910-915 (INQUIRY_RATE_LIMIT_MAX_IPS = 100_000, built with `with_default_bounded`) is explicitly documented to 'Bound memory against an attacker rotating source IPs ... the map never exceeds this many entries.' The price_map cache, keyed on an equally attacker-influenced string space, has no equivalent bound. Fix (backend-only, cloud-landable): cap the map (bounded LRU / size-limited insert that evicts oldest once a MAX_ENTRIES ceiling is hit, mirroring the inquiry limiter), and/or normalise+reject out-of-allowlist city/property_type before they reach the key, and/or key the cache on a hash of validated inputs only. Add a unit test asserting the cache size stays <= MAX_ENTRIES after N distinct-city inserts within the TTL window.

backend/servers/reality-server/src/routes/price_map.rs:158-206 and backend/servers/reality-server/src/routes/listings.rs:700-706 both build their query text with `format!(...)` and then execute it via `sqlx::query(sqlx::AssertSqlSafe(sql))` / `sqlx::query_as::<_, _>(sqlx::AssertSqlSafe(sql))`. AssertSqlSafe is a deliberate opt-out of sqlx's compile-time/runtime SQL-safety checking — it tells sqlx 'trust me, this string is safe', disabling the one framework guard that would otherwise catch an interpolated-value injection.

Both sites are SAFE AS WRITTEN TODAY: listings.rs interpolates only the RICH_LISTING_SELECT const (:703) and binds all user values ($1 transaction_type, $2 limit); price_map.rs interpolates only `interval`, which at :109-123 is the result of a closed `match time_window_str.as_str()` that maps to fixed literals ('1 month'/'3 months'/'12 months'/'5 years') and returns 400 on anything else, so no user bytes reach the format string. This is a latent-footgun / refactor-smell finding, not a live injection.

Risk: the safety now rests entirely on reviewer vigilance that every current and FUTURE format! argument stays a constant or an allowlisted literal — the compiler no longer enforces it. A later edit that interpolates a less-controlled value (e.g. a sort column, a city, a dynamic WHERE fragment) into either `sql` would introduce SQL injection silently, with no macro error. Fix (backend-only, cloud-landable): add an explicit `// SAFETY: only <const>/<allowlisted literal> is interpolated; all user input is bound` comment at each AssertSqlSafe call documenting the invariant, or migrate the dynamic portions to sqlx::QueryBuilder so parameters are bound rather than interpolated. A guard comment keeps the opt-out auditable; QueryBuilder removes the footgun entirely.
